extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, screenwriting students, and storytellers studying scene and story composition
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and composing individual scenes and their beats for dramatic effect in screenplays and film, focusing on conflict, turning points, pacing, rhythm, and unity within the larger story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action/Reaction Beat Progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Each beat pairs an action by one character with a reaction by another; the action/reaction pattern should build a rapid progression of beats where each exchange 'tops' the previous beat, placing the relationship in greater risk and demanding more willpower and capacity to take painful actions while remaining in control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label each beat's action and reaction; ensure each exchange increases stakes or intensity (i.e., 'each exchange tops the previous beat'). Use the sequence of actions/reactions to escalate tension toward the Turning Point. The example from CASABLANCA shows an 11-beat sequence where each beat progressively endangers the relationship until the gap opens on the revelation in Beat 11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define Conflict (Step One)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify who drives the scene and what they want; determine the sources of antagonism to that desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the protagonist's driving desire for the scene and list antagonists (people, circumstances, or self). Example: 'Karin drives the scene... Her sources of antagonism are her husband and herself.' This clarifies stakes and intention for all beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note Opening Value (Step Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Record the value state (emotional/ethical/psychological) that opens the scene — the audience's initial expectation or hope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the opening value to measure the scene's change; e.g., hope fills the opening of Karin's scene. Noting this value helps evaluate how the scene shifts toward its closing value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break the Scene into Beats (Step Three)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the scene into discrete beats (units where action/reaction changes the relationship dynamic) and define the action and reaction for each beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write beats as short exchanges with labelled character action and reaction (e.g., 'RICK — Your story left me a little confused.' Action: EXCUSE MAKING. ILSA — Reaction: REJECTING RICK'). Use beats to expose subtext and to test if behavior follows desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note Closing Value and Compare with Opening Value (Step Four)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the scene's closing value and compare it to its opening value to assess the degree and direction of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize whether the scene moved from positive to negative (or vice versa) and how sharply. This comparison reveals the magnitude of the scene's effect on the larger story (e.g., a shift from hope to hopelessness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey Beats and Locate the Turning Point (Step Five)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the beat sequence to find the Turning Point — the beat where a decisive gap or reversal occurs that changes the scene's trajectory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for where the chain of escalating beats 'opens a gap' (e.g., revelation or act of power). The Turning Point must be located within the beat progression and explains the change in closing value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict Necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-written scene must contain conflict: desires in opposition or obstacles that prevent easy achievement of goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid scenes that lack conflict; common flaws include absence of opposed desires, antiprogressive repetition, or lopsidedness where one side never resists. If desires aren't opposed, rewrite to create opposition or stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressivity of Action (Avoid Anti-Progressive/Circular Beats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes should be progressive — each action should move the scene forward; avoid repetitious or circular action that stalls progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each beat demands more and places stakes higher. Antiprogressive scenes repeat the same material or circle without escalation; such scenes need reworking to change behavior or desire to restore forward motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of Turning Point
rubrics_metrics.description: The Turning Point's timing within the scene matters: it must not come too early or too late relative to the scene's purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Turning Point that is too early or too late makes a scene feel lopsided. Use beat surveying to test whether the Turning Point arrives at the emotionally and logically appropriate moment to maximize impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and Subtext (Avoid 'On the Nose' Dialogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue and action must feel credible and convey subtext rather than stating everything explicitly; avoid 'on the nose' exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure actions and lines have subtext and believable motivation. Scenes lacking credibility (e.g., unrealistic reactions, explicit telling) undermine emotional impact. Use implicit behavior to convey truth without blunt statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and Variety (Canon of Composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story must be unified (causal lock between Inciting Incident and Story Climax) while offering as much variety as possible (tone, mood, subplot contrasts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure causal inevitability: 'Because of the Inciting Incident, the Climax had to happen.' Within that unity, vary tone (tragic/comic/political/personal) and use research/knowledge to avoid monotony and add richness (e.g., CASABLANCA mixes love story, politics, comedy, and music).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing (Tension and Release)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pacing balances cycles of tension and relaxation over scenes, sequences, and acts so the audience neither becomes exhausted nor numbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid turning the screw too slowly (which tires the audience) or keeping unrelenting pressure (which numbs them). Use act structure to raise and lower tension, creating cycles that build overall toward climaxes while allowing respiration between peaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and Tempo
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm is set by scene length (how long we're in the same time/place); tempo is the level of activity within a scene (dialogue/action intensity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Average film scenes tend to be two to three minutes; vary scene lengths to create pulse. As you approach act climaxes, shorten scene lengths while increasing tempo to accelerate momentum; conversely, let major climactic scenes breathe (longer, slower, tense). Avoid redundancy of shots in overly long scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of French Scenes and Sublocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Within a location, changes in character entrances/exits or sub-locations can define new 'French Scenes' and create rhythmic variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit entrances and exits to recompose relationship dynamics and create fresh scene beats even within one set (e.g., TWELVE ANGRY MEN uses many French Scenes within a jury room to vary rhythm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Earn the Pause before Climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Before major reversals or climaxes, the storyteller must 'earn the pause' — telescoping rhythm and spiraling tempo so a final slow, long scene holds the audience's breath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not place long, slow scenes of minor importance immediately before the major Climax — that dulls the Climax. Build acceleration (shorter scenes, higher tempo) so that when you brake for the Climax, the pause is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning Point Type: Revelation vs. Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning Points can pivot on revelation (an unveiled truth) or on action (a deed of power); the nature of the Turning Point should fit the scene's conflict and protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the type that best serves the story: Casablanca's Turning Point pivots on revelation (Ilsa's secret marriage), while THROUGH A GLASS DARKLY pivots on an action of the subconscious. Ensure the Turning Point feels credible in context and arises logically from beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of Composition (list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition is guided by an evolving set of canons: Unity and Variety, Pacing, Rhythm and Tempo, Social and Personal Progression, Symbolic and Ironic Ascension, and the Principle of Transition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these canons as a checklist when ordering and linking scenes: maintain unity of cause and effect, vary tone and subplots, pace acts and scenes to manage tension, progress characters socially and personally, build symbolic/ironic meaning across scenes, and ensure smooth transitions between scenes and sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene Length vs. Visual Expressivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Most directors find two or three minutes in a single location yields most visual expressivity; overly long scenes risk shot redundancy and loss of audience interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a scene must be long, justify it dramatically (e.g., a climactic scene may be long and slow). Otherwise, break or shorten scenes to maintain visual interest; remember formatted screenplay page≈minute guideline when planning scene lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Cliché while Respecting Technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A technique that becomes cliché still often works because it expresses something important; do not ignore proven techniques out of fear of cliché.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply classical techniques (shortening scenes to accelerate pace, pacing for climax, rhythmic cycles) with awareness; innovate only when you understand the effect you are replacing.
